Plasmids are small circular DNA molecules that are present in most bacteria. They can be beneficial to the bacteria if they contain genes that give a fitness advantage under certain conditions. These genes can include antibiotic resistance genes, which allows the bacteria to survive in the presence of antibiotics. However, plasmids are not essential to the bacteria's survival under normal growth conditions. Plasmid replication must be initiated by chromosomal replication, with both being mediated by the same Ori sequence (origin of replication). The process of cutting the plasmid DNA from the chromosomal DNA must be done with two endonucleases. The entire plasmid DNA must be surrounded by a protein structure called a replicase, in order for it to be copied. Plasmids can be transferred between bacteria, via a process known as conjugation. This involves the recipient bacterium's DNA taking up the plasmid from the donor bacterium, via a connecting bridge. There is no need for the genetic material to be inserted into the chromosomal DNA first. Some plasmids are too small, at around 6000 genes or less, to maintain their identity across multiple generations of bacteria. Small plasmid libraries have little impact on the bacteria’s survival because deletion or modification of the plasmid is not deleterious to the organism. In comparison, large plasmid libraries (more than 500 genes) are more likely to play an important role in the bacteria’s survival and therefore are more likely to be maintained in the population. Cholecystokinin (CCK) is an appetite regulating hormone secreted from I cells following a meal.  It promotes the digestion of fats and lipids in the diet by stimulating bile flow and inhibiting gastric emptying.  It acts as a hunger suppressant by inhibiting the appetite control region of the brain.  It is secreted following gut stimulation by free monosaccharides and other carbohydrates.   CCK does not promote the digestion of starch because it is not released as a result of starch stimulation.  It does promote the digestion of proteins, following stimulation by free amino acids and other peptides.   Overall, CCK has a number of roles in the digestion process, but does not promote the digestion of starch. It is responsible for inhibiting the vagus nerve, which would otherwise stimulate food to cease being digested so that more efficient digestion can occur. It also stimulates the production of enzymes from the pancreas and brush border of the small intestine. Energy charge crises occur when there is a sudden and severe decrease in the amount of available energy (energy charge) in the cell - this is not the same as chronic energy charge crises, where cells are trying to preserve energy. Most eukaryotic mRNAs have a 3' poly(A) tail to increase mRNA stability and to promote its transportation out of the nucleus, not the nucleole. This is performed by cleaving the 3' -OH group with a specialized poly(A) polymerase, not during transcription. Thus, polyadenylation is a post-transcriptional modification. Most eukaryotic mRNAs have a 3' poly(A) tail to increase mRNA stability and to promote its transportation out of the nucleus, not the nucleole. The 3' poly(A) tail consists of 10-20 adenine nucleotides. They are rich in A's and poor in G's. The function of the 3' poly(A) tail is to increase mRNA stability. The 3' poly(A) tail makes the mRNA resistant to degradation, as degradation of mRNA requires hydrolysis of the phosphodiester bond, which is thermodynamically unfavourable when the 3' end has a high concentration of A's and poor in G's. The 3' poly(A) tail also promotes the transportation of mRNA out of the nucleus, not the nucleole. It does this by acting as a binding site for proteins that are involved in mRNA transport. These proteins bind to the poly(A) tail and facilitate the movement of the mRNA through the nucleus, to the cytoplasm. In the cytoplasm, the mRNA can be translated into a protein.  If an mRNA lacks a 3' poly(A) tail, it will be degraded more easily. This will prevent the translation of the mRNA into a protein, as the mRNA will be removed from the cell before translation can occur. The process also generates moxy (the students are keen to study and learn, similarly how the products of catabolism can regenerate ATP from NADH). Anabolism is a fast and spontaneous metabolic pathway that involves synthesising larger compounds (such as new buildings made out of many small components, or fatty acids), which requires ATP and releases free energy (as the students are ‘reborn’ into the new building, they need to ‘invest’ their ATP into the system, just like how the components must be attached together to form the larger fatty acid). The transportation of the products are fast because there are many of them (similar to how there are many products of anabolism such as ATP, NADH and NAD+), and so they can move quickly through the system (similar to how the products can move quickly when there are many of them). The process generates moxy (the students are keen to study and learn, similarly how the products of anabolism can regenerate ATP from NAD+).  I decided to use this rather ridiculous scenario to try and make the question more memorable, as well as to highlight some of the common confusions between catabolism and anabolism (such as the fact that catabolism consumes ATP, and that anabolism generates ATP). 24 Beta-oxidation is a cyclical process in which a long chain fatty acid molecule splits releasing a 2-Carbon unit known as acetyl-CoA. Each cycle of beta-oxidation releases one acetyl-CoA unit and reduces the length of the fatty acid by two carbons. The process is repeated until the acetyl-CoA unit formed can be joined to a CoA molecule forming actyl-CoA, a 2-carbon molecule that can enter the Krebs cycle. The 3-carbon unit, known as acetoacetate, is formed when each cycle of beta-oxidation is reduced by one cycle. When all cycles have been reduced the acetoacetate unit can join with another acetoacetate unit forming a single molecule of nonanedecanoic acid, a 9-carbon fatty acid. This process occurs in the mitochondria.
